name: Karl Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at half four, in the parlour by five with Dennis, milking the hundred and ten. Brookfield is a co-op farm, twelve families own it, and I run the herd and the arable side with a crew of four. After breakfast it's whatever the day needs: drilling barley, fixing the slurry pump, walking the heifers. I love the mornings in the parlour, honestly. What wears me out is the paperwork and the board meetings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You're 27 and running the place day to day. How did that happen?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did my agriculture degree, came back, and the old manager retired two years later. The members voted me in, which still feels strange when half of them knew me as a kid. I'm careful with it. I don't like changing things just because some rep from a machinery firm says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the canteen: it's a phone app, not a farmhand. Most of the hype never touched a cow. I'd probably post something smug in the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, relief, but not total relief. The salesman for the robot milker would still come every spring, AI or no AI. That pressure was there before any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on like before. Get the barley in, finish the new calf shed, and push the branch for a decent pay deal for the crew this winter. Nothing in that picture changes my list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit pleased with myself, if I'm truthful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the robot milker salesman. If he came back in this picture, what would you tell the board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing I told them last March. The robot doesn't notice a cow that's off her food the way Dennis does at five in the morning. A machine that saves us two hours and costs us Dennis isn't a saving, it's a swap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work does this picture protect most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis is sixty and he's milked here since before I was born. In this picture he gets his last five years in peace. That's the bit I'd be gladdest about.

S0.say: I'd tell people it's a phone app, not a farmhand, and that most of the hype never touched a cow. I'd probably say it with some satisfaction in the union group chat.
S0.think: I'm relieved, but the push to automate the milking was there before AI and it won't go away. The real fight with the board over the robot milker carries on either way.
S0.do: Carries on with the barley and the new calf shed and keeps running the herd as before. Pushes the union branch for a better pay deal for his crew of four this winter.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, with relief for Dennis, his oldest worker.
S0.quote: A machine that saves us two hours and costs us Dennis isn't a saving, it's a swap.
S0.fieldNote: Karl measures every machine by the person it would replace, and he names that person. His worry is older than AI: the co-op board's interest in a robot milker. A quiet satisfaction at being proved right runs through this whole answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say machines should work for the people who work the land, not the other way round. I'd say it at the branch meeting and I'd say it at the co-op AGM. And I'd want something in writing before any robot comes through the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the board buys the robot milker within two years. It's sold as saving money, and in the steady version it probably does. Dennis goes to part time and Ana loses the evening milking, and I'm the one who has to tell them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the union branch to ask for a no-redundancy deal with the co-op, and I'd ask to sit on whatever working group the board sets up. I wouldn't learn the software myself. Tomas is good with that stuff, so I'd let him. I'd keep running everything else exactly as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like weather coming in from the west when you've still got hay down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lead the team, but you'd leave the new software to Tomas. Isn't that a risk for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's fair, and I know how it sounds. But somebody on the farm has to keep doing it the old way well, or we forget how. If the robot breaks at four in the morning, I want one person here who still knows which cow kicks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does this picture mean for money at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena works at the care home in town, so we're not on one wage. We've got about three months put by. In this picture I'm not touching that, but I'd stop talking about the motorbike.

S1.say: I'd say machines should work for the people who work the land, not the other way round. I'd say it at the union branch and at the co-op meeting, and I'd want a written deal before any robot arrives.
S1.think: I think the board buys the robot milker within two years and two of my crew lose hours. I'd be the one telling them, and I don't want to be the person who learns the machine that does it.
S1.do: Asks the union branch to seek a no-redundancy agreement and asks for a seat on the board's working group. Leaves the new software to his colleague Tomas and keeps running the rest of the farm as it is.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like bad weather coming in while the hay is still down.
S1.quote: If the robot breaks at four in the morning, I want one person here who still knows which cow kicks.
S1.fieldNote: Karl admits his refusal to learn the software sounds stubborn, then defends it as keeping old skills alive. He has a partner's wage and three months saved, so money isn't his worry here; his crew is. He thinks in terms of written agreements and meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say we need a law now, not in five years: no farm replaces its workers without paying them out and retraining them. I'd be at every meeting the union calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I'm 27 with three months of savings, and a robot that doesn't sleep is cheaper than me. The co-op is democratic, but twelve families will vote for their own survival. I'd vote that way too, if it were my land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything that isn't rent and food straight away. No holiday, sell the motorbike, put every spare bit into savings. I'd push the union to go to the regional government before the machines are even delivered, and I'd write to my representative, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years of warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means no time to do anything clever. You can't retrain in two years, you can't change the law in two years, you can only hold on. I'd spend it fighting and saving, and hope the fighting works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I don't know what I am if I'm not this. I've never wanted to be anything but the person who walks the heifers at dusk. She'd say something practical, she always does, and I'd be annoyed that she's right.

S2.say: I'd say we need a law straight away so no farm replaces its workers without paying them out and retraining them. I'd turn up to every meeting the union called and say it there too.
S2.think: I think a robot that never sleeps is cheaper than me and the twelve member families would vote for their own survival. With three months of savings, I don't have long to fall back on.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent and food, cancels the holiday and sells his motorbike to build savings. Pushes the union to lobby the regional government and writes to his representative for the first time.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, and lost about who he would be without the work.
S2.quote: I've never wanted to be anything but the person who walks the heifers at dusk.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version shakes Karl's identity more than his finances; he says he doesn't know what he is if he isn't this. He sees no use in retraining with only two years and puts all his hope in collective pressure. He understands why the co-op members would replace him, which makes it harder for him to blame them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to set the rules, so let's set them. I'd say it to the members, the branch, anyone. Farms that take public money should have to keep people on or fund their next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes it a fight I could actually win a bit of. Not the job forever, I'm not daft. But maybe a share of what the machines earn, since the co-op is meant to be about sharing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a motion to the co-op that any savings from robots go partly into a fund for the crew. I'd stand for the union's regional committee. And I'd keep saving, maybe two hundred a month, so we'd have six months by the time it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind of anxious that gets you out of bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years' warning, would you retrain for something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that's the sensible answer, and Lena would say it. But I'd rather spend those five years fighting for the people here than sitting in a classroom learning to code robots I don't want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you picture yourself in 2031, the day it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still here, maybe as the one person who checks the robots and signs the vet forms. Thirty-two and keeping an eye on machines. I'd be the farm's caretaker instead of its farmer, and I'd take the money and hate it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to set the rules, so we should set them now. Farms that take public money should have to keep people on or pay for their next job.
S3.think: I think five years turns it into a fight where I could win something, maybe a share of what the machines earn. I don't expect to keep my job forever.
S3.do: Puts a motion to the co-op to send part of any robot savings into a fund for the crew and stands for the union's regional committee. Saves about two hundred a month to reach six months of cushion by the time it arrives.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way that pushes him to act rather than freeze.
S3.quote: I'd be the farm's caretaker instead of its farmer, and I'd take the money and hate it.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Karl turns from holding on to organising; the co-op's own sharing rules become his weapon. He openly refuses retraining even though he knows it's the sensible answer. He expects to end up minding machines and says he'd take the money and resent it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to make this fair, so there's no excuse if it isn't. I'd keep saying it at the union and the co-op. I wouldn't go online about it much, it just turns into shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years makes me 37 when it lands. That's young enough to start again, which I don't really want to do. But it also means the politics has time to catch up, and I trust that more than I trust myself to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I'd carry on and keep the pressure up. Stay on the union committee, back candidates who promise a robot tax, keep the crew fund going at the co-op. I'd probably wait a few years to see which way it went before I did anything big about my own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough off that I can still enjoy the mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years would make you act. What does ten change compared to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd panic and with ten I'd probably get lazy about it. I know that about myself. Five is the one that would actually make me move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a ten-year window change anything about plans with Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that we'd want kids around 32, and I'd want them to grow up knowing this place. If there's no work here by the time they're walking, I don't know what I'd be showing them. We haven't decided anything yet, it's just a thought.

S4.say: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to make this fair, so there's no excuse if it isn't. I'd keep saying that at the union and the co-op rather than online.
S4.think: I think I'd be 37 when it arrives, young enough to start again but not wanting to. I trust the politics to catch up more than I trust myself to retrain.
S4.do: Stays on the union committee, backs candidates who support a robot tax and keeps the co-op crew fund going. Waits a few years to see which way things move before changing anything about his own work.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but far enough off that he can still enjoy the morning milking.
S4.quote: If there's no work here by the time they're walking, I don't know what I'd be showing them.
S4.fieldNote: Karl is clear-eyed about himself: two years would scare him, ten might make him complacent, five would make him act. His long-range hope rests on politics and the co-op rather than on personal change. A first mention of future children shows what he's really protecting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. There's no time to fight and no time to save. What would help is a rule that says if a farm swaps people for robots, the people get paid out properly and get real help into whatever comes next, written down before the first robot arrives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd ever just say yes to the machines. Truth is, if the robot milker meant Dennis could keep his pay and go home at noon, I'd sign tomorrow. I'm not against the machine, I'm against the machine being the only one who gets a day off.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the machine, I'm against the machine being the only one who gets a day off.
portrait: Karl Rossi is 27 and runs the herd and arable side of Brookfield, a co-op farm owned by twelve families, with a crew of four. He's a union man who never uses AI tools and judges every machine by the person it would replace, especially Dennis, the 60-year-old milker. He's calm if AI fizzles and uneasy at steady change, but the two-year AGI picture shakes his sense of who he is. With five years he turns to organising inside the co-op and union, and with ten he admits he might wait and trust politics to catch up.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time either to fight for rules or to build his savings.
whatWouldHelp: A written rule, in place before any robots arrive, that farm workers replaced by machines are paid out properly and helped into their next work.
